title: The Complete Guide to Label Terms
quiz.0.question: What is the minimum ageing requirement for Barolo Riserva?
quiz.0.explanation: Barolo Riserva needs at least 62 months' ageing (5+ years), 24 months more than the 38 months of the basic wine.
quiz.1.question: What does the term "Superiore" mainly stress?
quiz.1.explanation: Superiore mainly stresses higher alcohol (usually +0.5-1% ABV), indicating riper grapes, and often also a longer ageing requirement.
quiz.2.question: Among sparkling-wine sweetness terms, which is sweeter than Brut?
quiz.2.explanation: Extra Dry (12-17 g/L) is sweeter than Brut (6-12 g/L) — a historical naming quirk that often causes confusion.
quiz.3.question: Where must the grapes for Chianti Classico Gran Selezione come from?
quiz.3.options.0: Anywhere in the Chianti Classico area
quiz.3.explanation: Gran Selezione (first released in 2014) requires grapes from the estate's own vineyards and at least 30 months' ageing; since 2021 it also requires at least 90% Sangiovese and may show a UGA village name. It is the top tier of Chianti Classico.
slides.0.title: The Complete Guide to Label Terms
slides.0.subtitle: Cracking every secret of the Italian label — ageing, classification and sparkling-wine terms
slides.1.title: Ageing Terms: Riserva · Superiore · Classico
slides.1.content:
The Three Core Terms

Riserva (reserve) — longer ageing | Barolo: 38→62 months (+24) | Barbaresco: 26→50 months | Brunello: 50→62 months | Chianti Classico: 12→24 months. Usually made from the best grapes and vintages, a step above the basic wine
Superiore (superior) — higher alcohol (grape ripeness), usually +0.5-1% ABV | Valpolicella Superiore: 11→12%, at least 12 months' ageing | Soave Superiore: 10.5→11.5%. It stresses ripeness, not simply ageing
Classico (classic) — grapes from the historic core of the area, usually the most representative terroir | Examples: Chianti Classico DOCG (between Florence and Siena), Soave Classico (volcanic soils), Valpolicella Classico (the three historic valleys)
slides.2.title: The Classification Pyramid and the IGT Super Tuscans
slides.2.content:
DOCG

Top tier | about 77 | the strictest quality testing

Chemical + sensory tests for every batch / neck seal (fascetta) / examples: Barolo, Brunello, Amarone

DOC

Middle tier | about 330 | regulated

Must pass chemical and sensory analysis / grapes, yields and methods regulated / examples: Barbera d'Asti, Soave, Valpolicella

IGT

Geographical indication | about 118 | freedom to innovate

Non-traditional grapes allowed (Cabernet, Merlot) / the Super Tuscans / Italy's most expensive wine may be an IGT / example: Toscana IGT

Vino

Table wine | no geographical indication | no restrictions

The most basic tier / no grape or origin requirements / many have now moved up to IGT

An IGT Legend: the Super Tuscans

Tignanello (Toscana IGT) | Sassicaia (originally Vino da Tavola, with its own Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC since 2013) | Ornellaia (Bolgheri Superiore DOC) | these wines match top DOCGs in quality and reputation
slides.3.title: Sparkling-Wine Terms: Method and Sweetness
slides.3.content:
Italian sparkling wines are made by three main methods, and the sweetness terms follow a pattern that is easy to confuse.

Metodo Classico (traditional method)

  • Method: second fermentation in bottle (as in Champagne)
  • Aromas: yeast, toast, butter, nuts
  • Bubbles: fine and persistent
  • Ageing potential: 5-15 years
  • Main areas: Franciacorta DOCG, Trento DOC, Alta Langa DOCG

Metodo Charmat (tank method)

  • Method: second fermentation in large sealed stainless-steel tanks
  • Aromas: fresh fruit, flowers (no yeasty notes)
  • Bubbles: lively and fresh
  • Ageing potential: drink within 1-3 years
  • Main areas: Prosecco DOC/DOCG, Asti DOCG (sweet), Lambrusco
Dosaggio Zero / Brut Nature: 0-3 g/L | bone dry
Extra Brut: 0-6 g/L | very dry
Brut: 6-12 g/L | the most common dry style
⚠️ Extra Dry: 12-17 g/L | sweeter than Brut (a common misunderstanding!)
slides.4.title: Combined Terms and Grape Labelling in Practice
slides.4.content:
Combined terms and grape-labelling rules are the most important label-reading skills when choosing Italian wine.

Chianti Classico Gran Selezione

  • Created: first released in 2014 (the top tier of Chianti Classico)
  • Requirement: grapes must come from the estate's own vineyards
  • Ageing: at least 30 months; since 2021 at least 90% Sangiovese, and UGA village names may be shown
  • Quality goal: to stand alongside Brunello and Barolo
  • Examples: Fontodi, Fèlsina, Castello di Ama, Mazzei

Grape-Labelling Rules

  • Single variety: one grape named on the label → at least 85% of that grape
  • DOCG exception: Brunello di Montalcino must be 100% Sangiovese
  • IGT freedom: non-traditional grapes such as Cabernet and Merlot may be used
  • Common examples: Etna Rosso = 80%+ Nerello Mascalese | Friuli Pinot Grigio = 85%+ Pinot Grigio
  • Estate bottling: look for "Imbottigliato all'origine", a sign of better quality control
slides.5.title: 🍷 Term Example: Riserva
slides.5.caption: Banfi Riserva Chianti Classico DOCG 2010 — the label clearly shows "Riserva", meaning longer ageing than the basic wine and usually better grapes.
slides.6.title: 🍷 Term Example: Superiore
slides.6.caption: Papagena Barbera d'Alba Superiore 2010 — "Superiore" stresses higher alcohol and grape ripeness, not simply ageing time.
slides.7.title: 🍷 Term Example: Gran Selezione
slides.7.caption: Castello Fonterutoli Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG 2013 (Mazzei) — the top tier of Chianti Classico; grapes must come from the estate's own vineyards, with at least 30 months' ageing.
slides.8.title: 🍷 Term Comparison: Prosecco DOC vs Prosecco Superiore DOCG
slides.8.caption: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG — a step above ordinary Prosecco DOC, limited to the core hill area, with stricter rules on alcohol and quality.
slides.9.title: 🍷 Term Example: Metodo Classico
slides.9.caption: Franciacorta DOCG — made by the traditional method (Metodo Classico) with second fermentation in bottle, as in Champagne, in contrast to the Charmat tank method used for Prosecco.
slides.10.title: Key Takeaways
slides.10.points.0: Riserva requires longer ageing and is usually made from the best grapes and vintages
slides.10.points.1: Superiore stresses higher alcohol (grape ripeness), Riserva stresses ageing time; both can appear together
slides.10.points.2: Classico means the historic core of an area and usually its most representative terroir
slides.10.points.3: Chianti Classico Gran Selezione (2014) is the top tier, requiring estate vineyards and 30 months' ageing
slides.10.points.4: Italy's classification pyramid: DOCG (77, strictest testing) > DOC (330) > IGT (118) > Vino
slides.10.points.5: IGT allows non-traditional grapes; Super Tuscans (such as Tignanello) are mostly IGT and match top DOCGs in quality and reputation; Sassicaia gained its own DOC in 2013
slides.10.points.6: Metodo Classico (bottle fermentation) = complex, age-worthy / Metodo Charmat (tank fermentation) = fresh, early drinking
slides.10.points.7: Sparkling sweetness is easily misread: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut (12-17 g/L vs 6-12 g/L)
slides.10.points.8: Grape-labelling rule: one grape named on the label → at least 85% of that grape (a DOCG may be stricter)

slides.11.questions.4.question: What does "Classico" mean on an Italian label?
slides.11.questions.4.options.1: Grapes from the historic core of a DOC/DOCG
slides.11.questions.4.explanation: "Classico" means the grapes come from the historic original core of a DOC/DOCG (such as Soave Classico or Chianti Classico), usually the traditional heartland of higher quality.
